title: LLMs as Writing Assistants: Exploring Perspectives on Sense of Ownership and Reasoning
venue: The Third Workshop on Intelligent and Interactive Writing Assistants (In2Writing '24)
extended_summary:
This paper examines how people perceive ownership, contribution, and authorship when using large language models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT for writing. The authors focus on two questions: whether sense of ownership differs for creative versus non-creative writing, and how LLM use affects the relationship between perceived ownership and self-declared authorship. The study is not an intervention trial on writing performance or motivation; rather, it is a short survey about attitudes and perceptions.

The approach was a brief survey administered to 35 participants. Survey items asked respondents whether they felt they contributed to LLM-assisted writing in general/non-creative tasks versus creative tasks, whether they would submit LLM-generated content under their own name, whether they felt they owned the content, and whether those ownership perceptions changed after being reminded of their role in prompting or editing the output. The paper reports descriptive percentages and distributions from these self-reports.

The participant group was predominantly university students aged 18-24, mostly from science backgrounds and described as relatively tech-aware. The paper lists author affiliations in Bangladesh, and the participant description indicates a university-student sample, but it does not describe any school-based classroom implementation, control group, or random assignment. There is no writing instruction experiment, no high-school sample, and no 25-versus-25 design.

The main conclusion is that participants reported greater perceived contribution and ownership in non-creative writing than in creative writing, where they credited the LLM more. The authors also found a mismatch between ownership and authorship: many participants were willing to claim authorship of LLM-generated content even when they did not feel they owned it. Reminding participants about their prompting and editing increased their reported sense of ownership. For the purposes of verifying an alleged 2026 motivation RCT with extreme effect size, this paper is clearly not that study and should be excluded from any quantitative synthesis of ChatGPT-based writing feedback effects in high school, because it contains no randomized trial, no high-school participants, and no motivation or writing achievement outcome statistics suitable for effect-size extraction.
quality_tier_rationale: Peer-reviewed workshop paper with a clear but very limited empirical method: a small descriptive survey (n=35) of perceptions, not an RCT or causal evaluation. It provides only one credibility criterion at best and has major limitations for effect estimation, population relevance, and internal validity.
impact_tier_rationale: Impact on educational outcomes is unclear because the study does not estimate effects on writing achievement or motivation using a controlled design. Reported results are descriptive perception shifts only, so any practical impact is indeterminate.

interventions.use_case: Survey study of ChatGPT/LLM writing assistants examining perceived ownership, authorship, and contribution in creative versus non-creative writing tasks.

finding.finding_summary: This paper does not report a randomized or quasi-experimental educational intervention on student motivation or writing achievement. Instead, it presents a brief cross-sectional survey of 35 mostly university-aged participants about perceived contribution, authorship, and ownership when using ChatGPT for writing. Descriptively, 51.5% initially said they did not own ChatGPT-generated content, 17.1% said yes, and after prompting/reminding about user contribution the ownership percentages shifted upward (e.g., 'Yes' increased to 28.6%; after editing reminders 62.9% claimed ownership), but no inferential tests, effect sizes, standard deviations, or confidence intervals are reported.
finding.measure: Survey responses on sense of ownership, self-declared authorship, and perceived contribution in creative vs non-creative LLM-assisted writing

finding.finding_summary: The paper concerns writing assistance conceptually, but it does not measure writing quality, writing scores, literacy gains, or any pre/post writing performance outcomes. There are therefore no original statistics on writing improvement and no effect size that could support inclusion in a quantitative synthesis of ChatGPT-based writing feedback effectiveness.
finding.measure: Writing performance outcomes not actually measured
